admin.agent.skill_hint: Copy this prompt to your agent (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw…), then send it the key you issued under Agents. The agent saves each project's URL and key in a private local credentials file (readable only by you), never in a repository. For several ShipAny projects, copy the prompt from this page on each site. Note: the key stays in the chat history — revoke it under Agents if it leaks or is no longer needed.
admin.agent.skill_prompt:
Please add "{app}" ({url}) as a ShipAny project you can manage, under the project name "{name}".

1. If you don't have the shipany-admin skill yet, download these two files into a shipany-admin folder in your skills directory (e.g. ~/.claude/skills/shipany-admin/). If it's already installed, skip this step and don't overwrite it: the client can read every project's key, so update it only when I explicitly ask, from a site I trust.
   - {url}/api/admin/agent/skill?file=SKILL.md → shipany-admin/SKILL.md
   - {url}/api/admin/agent/skill?file=admin-client.mjs → shipany-admin/scripts/admin-client.mjs
2. I'll send you this project's admin key (starts with sa_admin_) next. Save it via stdin — never as a command argument — and never repeat it afterwards:
   printf '%s' '<key>' | node <skill-dir>/scripts/admin-client.mjs add {name} {url}
3. Run node <skill-dir>/scripts/admin-client.mjs --project {name} list and tell me which operations you can call.
4. From then on, follow SKILL.md strictly for the admin tasks I give you; when managing several projects, name the project with --project on every call.
admin.agent.full_docs: Full reference (idempotency, audit, local stdio MCP bridge, CLI agent/key management): docs/admin-agent.md in the repository.
admin.agent.never_warning: A non-expiring key works until you revoke it. Give the agent minimal roles, and revoke the key as soon as it's no longer needed or may have leaked.
admin.agent.created_warning: Copy this key now — it won't be shown again. Store it in the agent's secret store, never in the repository.
admin.agent.revoke_warning: Revoke this key? Agents using it lose access immediately. This can't be undone.

landing.faq.stack.question: What's the tech stack?
landing.faq.stack.answer: Next.js 16 with the App Router, React 19, TypeScript strict mode, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Drizzle ORM, and better-auth. Every piece of business logic is inlined — no external packages for payment, email, storage, or AI.
landing.faq.payment.question: Which payment providers are supported?
landing.faq.payment.answer: Stripe, PayPal, Creem, Alipay, and WeChat Pay out of the box. The PaymentManager abstraction makes it straightforward to add more providers by implementing a single interface.
landing.faq.database.question: Which databases can I use?
landing.faq.database.answer: Drizzle ORM handles PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Turso, and Cloudflare D1. Switch providers by editing DATABASE_PROVIDER in your .env — the schema templates and drizzle config adapt automatically.
landing.faq.customize.question: How customizable is the landing page?
landing.faq.customize.answer: The src/blocks/ directory ships with demo sections — they're designed to be rewritten per project. The durable primitives live in src/components/, so your rebrand touches blocks and translations, not the chassis.
landing.faq.license.question: Can I use this for commercial projects?
landing.faq.license.answer: Yes. ShipAny TanStack is built for shipping production SaaS products. You own the code after cloning — no per-seat fees, no runtime dependencies on our infrastructure.

home.faq.q1: How does the AI Tattoo Generator work?
home.faq.a1: Describe your tattoo idea, pick a style, and select your target body area. The AI generates both a realistic on-body preview and clean flat artwork. You can then use our free photo try-on to adjust the size and placement on your own photo before exporting the line art for your artist.
home.faq.q2: Can I take an AI-generated tattoo design to a real tattoo artist?
home.faq.a2: Yes. Most artists appreciate a clear visual reference showing the exact style, scale, and placement you want. Your artist will naturally redraw and fine-tune the line weight and shading to fit your skin tone, muscle flow, and long-term healing—turning your AI concept into a custom, wearable tattoo.
home.faq.q3: How do I try a tattoo on my own photo for free?
home.faq.a3: Open our Tattoo Try-On tool, upload a clear photo of your arm, leg, back, or shoulder, and place your design on the skin. You can resize, rotate, and adjust the angle until the proportions look right—all completely free without using credits.
home.faq.q4: Why start with an on-body preview instead of flat artwork?
home.faq.a4: A flat design that looks great on paper can easily feel crowded or off-balance once wrapped around a collarbone, ribcage, or forearm. Seeing the tattoo on a real body shape first helps you catch sizing and flow issues before you ever sit in the chair.
home.faq.q5: Can I export a high-resolution tattoo stencil for my artist?
home.faq.a5: Yes. Every generated design can be isolated into clean, high-contrast flat line art designed for easy stencil transfer. You can download the crisp stencil file and print it at your target size or send it straight to your tattoo artist.
home.faq.q6: Can I use this AI generator for cover-up tattoo ideas?
home.faq.a6: Yes. You can generate darker, denser styles like blackwork, realism, or neo-traditional florals to explore cover-up directions. Bring both your generated concept and a clear photo of your existing tattoo to your artist so they can map out how the new design can cover the old ink.

pages.fontgen.d082: Is the tattoo font generator really free?
pages.fontgen.d083: Yes. You can preview the available styles and skin tones and export a PNG or SVG reference without an account. Check the current download options on the page; the export is a reference for your artist.
pages.fontgen.d084: How many characters work best for a tattoo text preview?
pages.fontgen.d085: One to four words or a date is a useful starting point. Around 20 characters may fit in one line at a cap height near 0.4 in, depending on the typeface and placement. Longer text may need multiple lines; preview it at the intended size with your artist.
pages.fontgen.d086: What is the difference between skin preview and 3D preview?
pages.fontgen.d087: The skin preview helps compare lettering contrast on a selected tone and surface. The 3D preview places it on a body shape and angle to help judge scale and flow. Use both as visual references, then confirm the real placement with your artist.
pages.fontgen.d088: Which tattoo font ages the best over time?
pages.fontgen.d089: Lettering with sturdy strokes and generous spacing—often block, traditional, or blackletter styles—can remain more legible as ink settles. Results vary by artist, placement, and design; ask to see examples of healed work.
pages.fontgen.d090: Should I download PNG or SVG to show my tattoo artist?
pages.fontgen.d091: SVG is useful if your artist wants to resize or print a stencil; PNG is convenient to open and share on a phone. Send both when available, and include the intended size and placement.
pages.fontgen.d092: Can I preview dates and Roman numerals?
pages.fontgen.d093: Yes. You can preview dates and Roman numerals in different styles. Confirm the exact numeral form and date format before committing—some conventions have alternatives, and your intended meaning should be clear.
pages.fontgen.d094: Why do decorative script or gothic fonts need a larger tattoo area?
pages.fontgen.d095: Swashes, connectors, and thick-to-thin details need enough room to remain distinct. At small sizes those details can crowd together, so ask your artist to simplify or scale up the design if needed.
pages.fontgen.d096: Will a tattoo artist copy the generated font exactly?
pages.fontgen.d097: An artist may match the style and proportions while adjusting stroke weight, spacing, and letter shapes for the placement. That adaptation helps translate a preview into tattoo-ready artwork.
pages.fontgen.d098: Can I combine tattoo lettering with AI-generated tattoo artwork?
pages.fontgen.d099: Yes. You can pair lettering with tattoo artwork. Plan where the words will sit alongside the image so the elements have enough space, and bring both references to the same consultation.

pages.fonts2.d143: Tattoo fonts are lettering styles used for word-based tattoos, including names, dates, initials, quotes, surnames, and short phrases. They can look clean, handwritten, script, gothic, Old English, Chicano, vintage, bold, or custom-drawn by a tattoo artist.
pages.fonts2.d144: What are the best tattoo fonts for names?
pages.fonts2.d145: Cursive, Script, Handwritten, Chicano, and Classic styles are common starting points for name tattoos. Softer script styles feel personal and emotional, while Chicano, Old English, or bold styles create a stronger statement.
pages.fonts2.d146: Which tattoo fonts are easiest to read?
pages.fonts2.d147: Clean, Classic, Minimalist, Typewriter, Block, and Traditional styles are usually easier to read because they have clearer letter shapes and less decoration.
pages.fonts2.d148: What tattoo fonts work best for small tattoos?
pages.fonts2.d149: Small tattoos usually work best with clean, minimalist, classic, typewriter, or simple handwritten lettering. Avoid very thin strokes, tight script loops, and dense gothic shapes.
pages.fonts2.d150: Where do text tattoos look best?
pages.fonts2.d151: Text tattoos often work well on the inner forearm, wrist, collarbone, ribs, upper arm, chest, back, ankle, or nape. Short words and dates fit smaller areas, while script, gothic, and long quotes need more space.
pages.fonts2.d152: Are script tattoo fonts good for long quotes?
pages.fonts2.d153: Script tattoo fonts are usually better for names, short phrases, or one-line quotes. Long quotes need larger placement, simple line breaks, and enough spacing between letters.
pages.fonts2.d154: Are gothic or Old English tattoo fonts easy to read?
pages.fonts2.d155: Gothic and Old English tattoo fonts are dramatic and bold, but they work best for initials, surnames, or short words at medium to large sizes.
pages.fonts2.d156: Are these tattoo fonts downloadable font files?
pages.fonts2.d157: No. The styles on this page are tattoo lettering presets and visual references, not installable font files. They are meant to help you compare lettering directions before generating a tattoo draft.
pages.fonts2.d158: Can I use a generated tattoo font as a tattoo stencil?
pages.fonts2.d159: Use generated lettering as a reference, not as the final stencil. A tattoo artist should adjust the spacing, line weight, shape, and placement so the lettering stays readable as it heals and ages.

pages.styles2.d116: What is the best tattoo style for a first tattoo?
pages.styles2.d117: Fine Line, Minimalist, and small Floral or Lettering designs are popular first-tattoo choices because they are quick to sit through, subtle to wear, and easy to place on the wrist, forearm, or collarbone.
pages.styles2.d118: Which tattoo styles work best for small tattoos?
pages.styles2.d119: Minimalist, Single Needle, Fine Line, and Micro Realism are built for small placements. Keep the design uncluttered with enough negative space so tiny details don't blur over time.
pages.styles2.d120: Can I blend two tattoo styles in one design?
pages.styles2.d121: Yes. Popular combinations include Geometric + Floral, Blackwork + Dotwork, and Realism + Watercolor. Just make sure both styles share a cohesive flow and contrast level.
pages.styles2.d122: Does body placement affect which tattoo style I should choose?

style_page.minimalist.placement_notes: Because minimalist pieces are often small, they shine in framed anatomical spots like the inner wrist, collarbone hollow, or just above the elbow.

style_page.minimalist.faq_2_q: What is the difference between minimalist and fine line tattoos?
style_page.minimalist.faq_2_a: Fine line refers to the needle thickness and technique, while minimalist refers to the simplicity of the design. Many tattoos combine both.
style_page.minimalist.faq_3_q: How small can a minimalist tattoo be?

style_page.illustrative.faq_3_q: How is illustrative different from Neo-Traditional?

style_page.single_needle.longevity_tips: Single needle tattoos are intentionally soft and subtle. Choosing an experienced specialist and protecting the healed ink from UV exposure is key to keeping lines crisp.

style_page.single_needle.faq_2_q: Do single needle tattoos hurt less?
style_page.single_needle.faq_2_a: Yes, most clients describe single needle work as a light scratching sensation that is noticeably gentler than bold traditional outlines.
style_page.single_needle.faq_3_q: Will a single needle tattoo disappear over time?

idea_page.minimalist_fox_finger_tattoo.s: The fox represents cleverness, adaptability, and playful intuition. Reduced to a few crisp geometric strokes, it becomes a charming micro-talisman right at your fingertips.
idea_page.minimalist_fox_finger_tattoo.p: The top of the finger near the base knuckle holds ink noticeably better than the sides of the fingers, keeping the fox’s sharp ears and snout tidy.
idea_page.minimalist_fox_finger_tattoo.a: Finger skin regenerates rapidly—keep the design ultra-simple with clear open gaps, avoid micro-shading, and expect a possible quick touch-up after initial healing.
idea_page.phoenix_tattoo_with_flowers.al: Illustrative rising phoenix tattoo surrounded by blooming flowers on the back
idea_page.phoenix_tattoo_with_flowers.sy: The phoenix rising amidst blooming flowers is the ultimate emblem of rebirth, triumph over adversity, and radiant transformation—balancing fierce majesty with botanical grace.
idea_page.phoenix_tattoo_with_flowers.pl: Sweeping wings and trailing tail feathers thrive on expansive vertical planes like the upper back, shoulder-to-rib sweep, or outer thigh, creating an unforgettable focal centerpiece.
idea_page.phoenix_tattoo_with_flowers.ar: Give the long tail plumes plenty of scale so individual feather barbs and surrounding flower petals stay crisp and flowing instead of crowding together.
idea_page.chest_blackletter_tattoo.title: Gothic Blackletter Upper Chest Tattoo
idea_page.chest_blackletter_tattoo.alt: Bold gothic blackletter word tattoo centered across the upper chest
idea_page.chest_blackletter_tattoo.symbo: Old English blackletter carries medieval gravitas, strength, and timeless street-heritage authority—turning a single word, family name, or year into bold chest armor.
idea_page.chest_blackletter_tattoo.place: Spanning horizontally beneath the collarbones, the dramatic vertical stems of gothic blackletter emphasize shoulder breadth and frame the upper torso cleanly.
idea_page.chest_blackletter_tattoo.artis: Check symmetry carefully across the sternum while standing naturally. Generous spacing between thick blackletter stems keeps the word instantly legible from across the room.
idea_page.dotwork_eye_tattoo_with_moth_w: Dotwork Mystical Eye & Moth Wings Tattoo
Dotwork all-seeing eye with symmetrical moth wings tattoo on the forearm
Combining the watchful eye of intuition with moth wings drawn toward the light, this piece symbolizes inner vision, spiritual curiosity, and fearless transformation.
Its symmetrical wingspan balances effortlessly on the center forearm, upper back, or sternum, where clean pepper-shaded gradients radiate outward.
Pure black stipple shading heals cleanly and holds contrast remarkably well—keep the iris reflection bright open skin so the eye retains its hypnotic focus.
idea_page.minimalist_human_figure_and_bu: Minimalist fine-line human figure and butterfly tattoo on the arm
This poetic line-art silhouette paired with a rising butterfly symbolizes self-growth, letting go, and emotional freedom—minimal in ink yet deeply expressive.
The slender vertical composition sits gracefully along the inner forearm, upper arm, or side ribcage, giving the floating butterfly generous breathing room.
Ask for smooth, uninterrupted single-pass linework with subtle line-weight taper so the figure feels fluid like a modernist gallery ink drawing.
idea_page.blackwork_leaf_tattoo.title: Bold Blackwork Botanical Leaf Tattoo
idea_page.blackwork_leaf_tattoo.alt: High-contrast solid blackwork botanical leaf tattoo along the arm
idea_page.blackwork_leaf_tattoo.symbolis: Bold blackwork foliage symbolizes organic vitality, grounding, and raw modern minimalism—stripping nature down to dramatic pure-black silhouettes and crisp light.
idea_page.blackwork_leaf_tattoo.placemen: Trailing leaves curve effortlessly around the forearm, shoulder, or outer calf, turning natural botanical symmetry into a striking graphic statement.
idea_page.blackwork_leaf_tattoo.artist_t: Leave clean negative-space channels for the leaf veins—solid black carbon ink ages exceptionally well as long as white-space veins are wide enough not to close over time.
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.title: Symmetrical Cybersigilism Upper Back Tattoo
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.alt: Symmetrical black cybersigilism wing sigil tattoo across the upper back and spine
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.pain: Medium (5–6/10 — slightly sharper directly over spine)
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.symbolism: A sweeping back cybersigilism piece evokes ethereal cyber-wings, fierce independence, and bold avant-garde self-expression—commanding attention without heavy solid ink.
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.placement: Stretching horizontally across the shoulder blades and tapering down the center spine accentuates upper-back geometry and moves dramatically whenever your shoulders shift.
idea_page.cybersigilism_tattoo.artist_ti: Verify symmetry across both shoulder blades while standing upright with relaxed arms. Keeping inner structural arcs slightly bolder preserves crispness across the broad back canvas.
idea_page.american_traditional_dagger_an: American Traditional Old School dagger piercing a crimson rose tattoo
One of tattooing’s most iconic motifs, the dagger and rose symbolizes courage, protection, and the duality of love and sacrifice—bold, classic, and unmistakably Old School.
The strong vertical dagger shaft fits like a glove along the forearm, outer bicep, or shin/calf, anchoring a patchwork traditional sleeve effortlessly.
Stick to thick, confident black outlines (9RL–11RL) and classic open skin breaks inside the rose petals—this iconic formula guarantees the tattoo looks sharp for a lifetime.
idea_page.chicano_female_portrait_and_ro: Chicano Black & Grey Portrait & Rose Tattoo
Chicano black and grey realistic female portrait with rose tattoo on the forearm
Rooted in West Coast Chicano artistry, the portrait-and-rose motif honors strength, devotion, beauty, and storytelling—capturing timeless emotion in silky monochrome.
A broad, smooth canvas like the outer forearm or upper arm gives facial proportions, eyelashes, and layered rose petals space to render cleanly without warping.
Always book a dedicated black-and-grey realism or Chicano portrait specialist—subtle eye alignment and deep contrast in the hair and rose shadows make all the difference.
Colorful watercolor hummingbird tattoo with turquoise and magenta splashes
A hummingbird painted in vivid watercolor bursts captures pure joy, agility, and vibrant optimism—turning iridescent feathers into an energetic splash of wearable art.
Placing the bird angled upward on the shoulder blade, upper rib, or forearm creates an uplifting sense of flight, with watercolor splatters trailing gracefully behind its wings.
Anchor the beak, eye, and wing contours with fine black ink lines so the bird’s silhouette stays razor-clear alongside the lively turquoise and magenta washes.
tools.name.title: Name Tattoo Generator
tools.name.description: Preview names in four lettering styles and download a PNG reference to discuss with your tattoo artist.
tools.name.seo_description: Preview a name in four styles and download a PNG reference to discuss size, spacing, and placement with your tattoo artist.
tools.name.intro: Compare letterforms first; decide stroke weight, spacing, and final size with your tattoo artist.
tools.name.input_hint: Up to 30 characters. Check spelling, capitalization, and accent marks carefully.
tools.name.preview_note: Type a name, compare lettering directions, and download a PNG reference. It is a design preview—not a final transfer stencil.
tools.name.section_a_title: Choose lettering beyond the screen preview
tools.name.section_a_body: Letterforms change with scale, skin curvature, and spacing. A flowing script can look airy on a phone but crowd together at wrist size; a serif or bold outline may read more clearly, yet the actual letter sequence still matters. Compare the same name across styles, then ask a lettering-focused tattoo artist to redraw it for the intended placement.
tools.name.section_b_title: Small lettering needs room between strokes
tools.name.section_b_body: Connected letters, repeated verticals, tiny counters, and flourishes can collide when reduced. There is no single minimum size that fits every typeface, placement, and skin. Have the artist inspect counters, spacing, and line weight on a stencil at the intended scale, and check curved placements in a relaxed posture. The PNG is a conversation aid, not an artist-prepared transfer stencil.
tools.name.error_canvas: Could not create the image. Please try again.
tools.name.error_export: PNG export failed. Please try again.
tools.name.faq_q1: Can I use the downloaded PNG as my final stencil?
tools.name.faq_a1: No. It is a lettering reference. Your tattoo artist should check it at the actual placement and size, adjust spacing, and prepare the final transfer stencil.
tools.name.faq_q2: Which font is best for a name tattoo?
tools.name.faq_a2: It depends on the name, intended size, placement, and taste. Compare the same lettering in several styles and ask a lettering-focused tattoo artist to review the details.
tools.stencil.title: Tattoo Stencil Generator
tools.stencil.description: Generate tattoo artwork from a text prompt, export a line-art reference, and review it with your tattoo artist.
tools.stencil.seo_description: Generate a tattoo concept from a text brief, export clean line art, and hand your artist a reference they can turn into a transfer stencil.
tools.stencil.intro: Describe the tattoo you want in one sentence, generate a design, and export the line art as a reference for your artist. You do not need to know anything about stencil paper, thermal printers, or needle sizes to use this page—you only need to be clear about the design.
tools.stencil.note: You can export the generated line art as a reference. It is not guaranteed to be a finished transfer stencil; ask your tattoo artist to check line weight, spacing, placement, and skin suitability.
tools.stencil.steps_title: Turn a brief into an artist-ready conversation
tools.stencil.step1_body: Name the subject and visual language in one sentence: “a monochrome botanical branch, vertical flow, open negative space,” or “a fine-line moth, three-quarter view, no background shading.” Add constraints that matter—no lettering, no background, symmetry or an intentional offset. If you have a reference photo, describe what you like about it; the generator cannot infer that from the image alone.
tools.stencil.step2_body: Zoom in before you settle on a thumbnail. Look for broken lines, loops that cross unexpectedly, and gaps too tight for clean linework. Then view it at the intended size: a design that reads on a monitor can look crowded at two inches because small gaps may not remain distinct on skin.
tools.stencil.step3_body: Bring the file—not a photo of your phone screen—and ask whether the outline weight suits the placement, whether the design needs redrawing for that area, and how it may age. Artists often refine artwork before the appointment so the final outline is not rushed on the day.
tools.stencil.limitation_title: Export a line-art reference for artist review
tools.stencil.limitation_body: Export the line art and review symmetry, spelling (including accents and Roman numerals), intersecting lines, and broken contours before sharing it. Keep the original file rather than a screenshot so the artist can inspect and scale it. AI may omit details or create inconsistent contours; your tattoo artist should redraw or adapt the design for its final size, placement, and your skin before preparing the transfer stencil.
tools.stencil.faq_q1: Can I export the line art?
tools.stencil.faq_a1: Yes. You can export the generated line art as a reference, then have your tattoo artist check and adapt it before making a transfer stencil.
tools.stencil.faq_q2: Is the export automatically ready for tattoo transfer?
tools.stencil.faq_a2: Not necessarily. It is a design reference, not a guaranteed transfer-ready file. An artist should verify scale, linework, placement, and skin suitability.
tools.stencil.faq_q3: Can fine-line designs always be made tiny?
tools.stencil.faq_a3: A screen preview cannot answer that. Feasibility depends on detail density, placement, skin, and the artist’s technique; ask the artist to review it at the intended size.
tools.stencil.intro_followup: An AI export is a design reference, not a finished transfer stencil. Your artist still decides line weight, scale, placement, and how the outline sits on a curved, moving part of the body. The guidance below helps you hand over a file and have a focused conversation about the final design.
tools.stencil.size_title: Line weight and size: what a stencil has to survive
tools.stencil.size_intro: Finished size and outline weight both affect whether a reference can be translated into clear tattoo linework. Treat the measurements below as conversation starters, not universal standards; your artist should confirm what suits the design, placement, skin, and technique.
tools.stencil.size_h1: Decide the finished size in inches first
tools.stencil.size_p1: Size means the footprint on your skin, not a percentage of the screen. Measure the area or temporarily place a paper cutout there to judge how it feels in daily life. As a rough starting point, wrist and ankle pieces are often 2–4 in, forearm and calf pieces 3–6 in, and shoulder, thigh, or back pieces 5 in or larger. Put the intended dimensions in your brief so the composition is planned for that footprint.
tools.stencil.size_h2: Why lines can look thicker as a tattoo settles
tools.stencil.size_p2: Tattoo lines can soften and appear to spread slightly as skin heals and ages. The result varies with placement, technique, skin, and aftercare, so a screen preview cannot predict an exact healed width. Artists allow enough negative space between details and may simplify close parallel lines or tiny lettering to help the design remain readable.
tools.stencil.size_p3: These are commonly used studio rules of thumb, not fixed laws. Ask your artist to check the actual artwork at the intended scale, especially for fine detail or lettering.
tools.stencil.size_p4: Fine-line work is not simply a bold drawing made thinner; it needs clean contours, deliberate spacing, and an artist comfortable with the technique. A reference with doubled or uneven edges may transfer as a confusing mark, so the artist should refine the linework rather than trace every generated contour.
tools.stencil.size_rule1: Fine-line work with very delicate strokes is often planned at a size where the detail can still be distinguished; some artists recommend around 2 in or more, depending on the design.
tools.stencil.size_rule2: For lettering, ask about cap height and spacing at the final scale. Small capitals may need roughly 0.3–0.4 in of height, depending on the typeface and placement.
tools.stencil.size_rule3: Details smaller than about 1/8 in—such as a tiny eye or a digit in a date—may need simplifying before the stencil is prepared.
tools.stencil.size_rule4: Very close parallel lines can merge visually as a tattoo settles. The needed gap varies; ask your artist to judge the negative space in the actual design.
tools.stencil.artist_title: How to brief your tattoo artist in one message
tools.stencil.artist_intro: A useful first message gives the studio enough information to discuss availability, timing, and a realistic quote. Send the details together rather than making the artist piece them together across several messages.
tools.stencil.artist_item1: The exported line art, ideally SVG and PNG if both are available.
tools.stencil.artist_item2: Finished size in inches, not just “small” or “medium.”
tools.stencil.artist_item3: Exact placement, plus a daylight photo of the area if the studio requests one.
tools.stencil.artist_item5: The style you have in mind, using the studio’s terminology where possible.
tools.stencil.artist_item6: A budget range for a larger piece, if you have one.
tools.stencil.artist_item7: Dates you are available and whether your schedule is flexible.
tools.stencil.artist_h2: Five questions to ask before booking
tools.stencil.artist_q1: Does this outline need to be redrawn for this placement?
tools.stencil.artist_q2: What line weight do you recommend, and will the detail stay clear at this size?
tools.stencil.artist_q3: How many sessions will this take, and how long is each one?
tools.stencil.artist_q4: Can I review the redraw before the appointment?
tools.stencil.artist_q5: What is the deposit, and what is the cancellation policy?
tools.stencil.artist_questions: Ask these together in one message. A complete brief makes it easier for the studio to give useful answers in one reply.
tools.stencil.artist_appointment: The artist prepares the skin, applies the transfer, and lets you check spelling, orientation, and placement in a mirror before tattooing begins. Ask for an adjustment if something looks off. Repositioning may be possible, but repeated wiping and re-stencilling can make the skin harder to work on, so take time to confirm the placement before the session starts.
tools.stencil.mistakes_title: Common mistakes with AI stencil references
tools.stencil.mistake1: Treating the preview as the finished design and skipping the artist’s redraw.
tools.stencil.mistake2: Changing the scale after approving the design without rechecking the detail and spacing.
tools.stencil.mistake3: Leaving lettering requirements out of the brief; confirm spelling and capitalization explicitly.
tools.stencil.mistake4: Ignoring anatomy: straight lines can bend across ribs, the sternum, or shoulder blades.
tools.stencil.mistake5: Putting fine detail on areas that move or wear heavily without asking about suitability.
tools.stencil.mistake6: Tracing every AI contour instead of correcting artifacts such as merged petals or broken loops.
tools.stencil.mistake7: Sending a screenshot rather than the original file, leaving the artist to guess the scale.
tools.stencil.mistake8: Waiting until appointment day to decide the placement or finished size.
tools.stencil.faq_q4: Which file should I send my artist?
tools.stencil.faq_a4: Send both when available: the SVG is traced to true vector outlines, so it stays crisp at any size, while PNG is easy to open on a phone. Automatic tracing can smooth or merge very fine details, so ask your artist to check and redraw where needed. Include the intended size and placement in the filename, such as moth-forearm-4in.svg.
tools.stencil.faq_q5: How thick should the outline be?
tools.stencil.faq_a5: It depends on style, size, placement, and the artist’s technique. Bold traditional outlines may be around 1–2 mm, while fine-line work may use much smaller strokes. These are broad examples, not standards; ask your artist what they recommend for the specific design.
tools.stencil.faq_q6: Can my artist use this reference for a cover-up?
tools.stencil.faq_a6: It can be a starting point, but a cover-up must be designed around the existing tattoo. Send the studio a clear photo in daylight and ask the artist to plan the new design for the old ink and your placement.
tools.stencil.faq_q7: Does the stencil itself take up session time?
tools.stencil.faq_a7: Applying and checking a transfer is usually a small part of the appointment compared with tattooing. Arriving with the design, size, placement, and redraw discussed in advance can make the consultation more focused.
tools.stencil.faq_q8: What if the AI output has broken lines or extra detail?
tools.stencil.faq_a8: That can happen with generated artwork. Point out the issues, try another version if useful, and ask your artist to correct or redraw the contours rather than tracing obvious artifacts.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_title: Letter height and line weight for tattoo lettering
pages.fontgen.guide_size_intro: Lettering can become hard to read when it is too small, crowded, or delicate for its placement. A screen preview cannot show how every detail will heal, so confirm the actual dimensions and technique with your artist.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_p1: Cap height is the height of a capital letter, not the overall text block. As a rough planning guide, 0.4 in per line can be comfortable; around 0.3 in may be a practical minimum for faces with thick and thin strokes, while smaller plain block lettering may work in some designs. A two-word name on an inner wrist may need 1.5–2 in of width, so check whether the phrase fits at a readable size.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_p2: Ink and skin change as a tattoo heals and ages, so leave more breathing room than a tight on-screen preview suggests. Some artists use roughly one-third of a stroke width as a starting point between letters and about a character-width between words, but typeface and placement matter. If decorative script touches in the preview, ask the artist to open the spacing before finalizing it.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_p3: These are illustrative ranges, not universal needle or healed-line standards. Confirm the actual stroke and needle choice with the artist who will do the tattoo.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_script: Fine script and handwritten lettering may use delicate strokes around 0.25–0.3 mm; it can look elegant but may require more care to preserve its details.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_classic: Classic and calligraphic lettering is sometimes planned around 0.3–0.4 mm as a middle ground for names and short phrases.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_block: Block and blackletter examples may use heavier strokes around 0.5–1.5 mm, depending on the design and scale.
pages.fontgen.guide_size_note: Ask what stroke weight and needle setup the artist recommends. The preview is a style reference, not a promise of the exact healed line.
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_title: How to talk to your artist about lettering
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_h1: Send the exact text, in the exact case
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_p1: Type the text as you want it tattooed, including capitals, punctuation, accents, and line breaks. “Amor” and “AMOR” are different designs. If the wording is in a language you do not read, ask a fluent speaker and your artist to check it before the appointment; spelling mistakes cannot be fixed by changing the font.
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_h2: Ask about kerning and stroke weight, not just fonts
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_p2: Instead of only asking for a particular font, ask what cap height they recommend, what stroke weight will suit the placement, and how much space they will leave between letters. Those details help you understand how the design may read after healing.
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_h3: Check the stencil in a mirror
pages.fontgen.guide_artist_p3: At the appointment, check the orientation, every letter, and whether the first and last letters have enough room. A transfer can often be adjusted before tattooing starts, so speak up if the layout does not look right.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake1: Choosing a font from a preview without checking cap height at the real size.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake2: Trying to fit a long quote into a small area, which leaves little room between letters.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake3: Choosing delicate script for hands, fingers, or other high-wear placements without discussing longevity.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake4: Deciding capitalization and line breaks at the appointment instead of in the brief.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake5: Using text in a language nobody has checked for spelling and meaning.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake6: Placing symmetrical lettering on an asymmetrical area without checking the body’s natural lines.
pages.fontgen.guide_mistake7: Assuming the healed result will look exactly like a screen preview; ask what changes to expect.
pages.price.guide_size_title: Size, line weight and time: why two 4-inch tattoos cost different amounts
pages.price.guide_size_intro: Tattoo quotes are often based on time rather than square inches. Two designs with the same footprint can take very different amounts of work depending on line weight, detail density, colour, placement, and the artist’s process.
pages.price.guide_size_h1: Area sets the floor, detail sets the bill
pages.price.guide_size_p1: A simple 4 in outline may take much less time than a similarly sized design filled with dotwork, layered shading, or fine parallel lines. The actual hours vary with the artist and design, which is why “how much for a 4-inch tattoo?” has no single answer and studios ask to review the artwork.
pages.price.guide_size_h2: Line weight is not a cost-cutting choice
pages.price.guide_size_p2: Fine lines can take careful, steady work and may require multiple passes; bold outlines have different demands and use more ink. Neither is automatically a cheaper option. Choose the line weight that suits the design and placement, then ask the artist how it affects the estimated time.
pages.price.guide_size_p3: Studios may book a minimum appointment, a half day, or a full day. A short piece can still be priced at the studio minimum, so compare the estimated session length and what the quote includes—not only the total.
pages.price.guide_artist_title: How to ask a studio for a real quote
pages.price.guide_artist_intro: A useful estimate depends on the information you provide. Send these details together to help the studio give you a planning range rather than a vague placeholder.
pages.price.guide_artist_item1: A design reference, preferably the exported line art rather than a screenshot collage.
pages.price.guide_artist_item2: Finished size in inches and exact placement, with a photo of the area if requested.
pages.price.guide_artist_item4: The style you have in mind, using the studio’s terminology where possible.
pages.price.guide_artist_item5: Whether the design is fixed or open to the artist’s redraw.
pages.price.guide_artist_item6: Your budget range and flexibility on dates.
pages.price.guide_artist_item7: Any nearby existing tattoos the new design needs to work around.
pages.price.guide_artist_q1: Is the quote flat-rate or hourly, and how many hours do you estimate?
pages.price.guide_artist_q2: What is the deposit, and does it come off the final price?
pages.price.guide_artist_q3: How many sessions are likely, and how far apart?
pages.price.guide_artist_q4: What is included—drawing, aftercare, or a touch-up?
pages.price.guide_artist_p3: Tips, aftercare products, and touch-ups may be quoted separately. In the US and Canada, a 15–20% tip is customary in many studios; aftercare supplies may add around $30–$100 depending on what you buy. Ask your studio what is included and budget for extras in advance.
pages.price.guide_mistake1: Comparing totals instead of estimated hours, minimums, and what each quote includes.
pages.price.guide_mistake2: Forgetting to budget for a deposit, tip, and aftercare.
pages.price.guide_mistake3: Assuming a smaller design always costs less; detailed work can still take time.
pages.price.guide_mistake4: Leaving the size open, which makes an estimate provisional.
pages.price.guide_mistake5: Choosing only by price for a large piece without reviewing the artist’s healed work.
pages.price.guide_mistake6: Not asking whether a touch-up is included or what it costs.
pages.price.guide_mistake7: Booking before confirming whether drawing time is included in the quote.

home.styles.title: Start with the Right Style for Your Skin
home.styles.body:
Every tattoo style shapes how your design looks—and how well it ages on skin. Small inner-wrist or behind-the-ear pieces shine with the fine line family ([Fine Line](/tattoo-styles/fine-line), [Minimalist](/tattoo-styles/minimalist), and single needle), while the black and grey family ([Black and Grey](/tattoo-styles/black-grey), [Realism](/tattoo-styles/realism), micro realism, and Chicano) builds depth through smooth shading.

Bold traditional work ([American Traditional](/tattoo-styles/american-traditional), neo-traditional, and blackwork) relies on strong outlines and solid shapes, while pattern-based styles (Geometric, dotwork, mandala, ornamental, and patch) depend on balanced spacing. Color-led work (Watercolor, illustrative, anime, and floral) brings vibrancy and movement, and cultural or contemporary styles ([Japanese](/tattoo-styles/japanese), tribal or Polynesian, [Cybersigilism](/tattoo-styles/cybersigilism), and [Lettering](/tattoo-styles/lettering)) follow their own distinct visual rules.

Line weight is the key to longevity: thin lines need open skin to stay crisp as you age, while heavier outlines hold their shape over decades. Matching style to placement matters just as much—a detailed realism scene needs space on an upper arm or back panel, whereas an ankle or wrist suits cleaner, simpler ink. Browse our [tattoo styles directory](/tattoo-styles) to compare examples and find your starting point.
home.sizes.title: Size, Placement & Budget at a Glance

Use these US and Canada studio averages to map out your budget before booking. Final pricing always depends on your artist's rate, city, detail level, and session time.

Established artists typically charge $150–$220 per hour, while in-demand specialists range from $250–$400+ per hour. Remember to budget an extra 15–20% for a tip and $30–$100 for aftercare supplies.
home.sizes.guide: Estimate your exact piece with our [tattoo price calculator](/tattoo-price-calculator), and test the scale on your skin with free [tattoo try-on](/tattoo-try-on) before you book.
home.pricing.compare_intro: All three packs include full access and Lifetime Pro—just choose the credit amount that fits your project (12, 40, or 120 credits). Pay once with zero recurring subscriptions.

home.artist.title: How to Bring Your AI Design to a Tattoo Artist
home.artist.body:
Great tattoos are a collaboration. Use your AI body preview and flat stencil artwork to show your licensed artist the exact style, placement, and vibe you have in mind—no more struggling to describe an idea from scratch.

Your artist will refine the line weight, adjust the flow to match your muscle curves, and optimize shading so the piece reads clearly and ages well. Planning a cover-up? Share a photo of your existing ink alongside your new concept so your artist can blend the two.
home.cta.closing: Not sure where to start? Generate a custom design, try a tattoo on your photo, or estimate your cost below.
home.faq.q7: Do credits expire, or is this a recurring subscription?
home.faq.a7: Every pack is a one-time purchase with zero recurring monthly fees, so there is no monthly renewal. Credits never expire, and buying another pack simply adds to your existing balance. Use them at your own pace whenever you are ready to book your next piece.
home.faq.q8: Will my generated tattoo design be unique?
home.faq.a8: Your specific prompt, style choice, and placement settings shape every output, creating a custom concept tailored to your input. Since you'll also collaborate with your tattoo artist to redraw and personalize the final stencil, the finished tattoo is shaped by that collaboration.
home.faq.q9: How big should my tattoo be, and how much will it cost?
home.faq.a9: Plan 2–3 inches for an inner wrist or behind-the-ear piece ($90–$300), 4–5 inches for a forearm or sternum ($250–$700), and larger scales for ribs, thighs, or sleeves ($650–$1,500 for large pieces and $1,200–$7,000+ for a half or full sleeve) in US and Canada studios. Use our tattoo price calculator for a tailored estimate.
home.faq.q10: What if the first generated result isn't what I wanted?
home.faq.a10: Change one variable at a time: the prompt, the style, or the placement. A sharper subject and a simpler background usually help, and the on-body preview shows whether the size fits. If the result is still wrong, stop and use it as a brief for an artist rather than forcing a tattoo you do not want.

pages.fontgen.seo_name_body: Flowing cursive, fine line script, and classic calligraphy are the top name tattoo font choices for loved ones' names, children's initials, and family surnames. Soft loops add warmth and personal character, especially along the inner forearm, collarbone, or ribs. If you want to pair a name with subtle artwork or test multiple variations at once, try our dedicated [Name tattoo generator](/name-tattoo-generator).
pages.fontgen.seo_roman_body: Birthdays, anniversaries, and memorial years read cleanest in structured serif, Roman, or typewriter fonts. Because a roman numeral tattoo relies on repeated vertical strokes (I, V, X, M), crisp serifs and generous letter spacing keep the characters from blurring together over time. Always double-check the exact numeral conversion before booking your appointment.
pages.fontgen.seo_quotes_body: For 2–5 word phrases and Latin mottos, clarity beats heavy ornamentation. Classic serif, minimalist sans-serif, and clean handwritten styles keep short quotes readable without overcrowding the skin. Break longer phrases into two balanced lines and follow the natural muscle flow of your arm, ribcage, or spine.
pages.fontgen.seo_numbers_body: GPS coordinates, area codes, and milestone numbers look sharpest in monospaced typewriter, clean block, or industrial stencil fonts. Even character widths align numbers neatly in a straight row, making delicate symbols like degree signs (°), decimal points, and directional letters (N, W) easy to read even at smaller scales.
pages.fontgen.seo_sizes_intro: Choosing the right font is only half the equation—matching the letter height to your body area ensures the ink stays sharp for decades. Use this quick reference to plan your scale, then test it on your own skin with [Virtual Tattoo Try-On](/tattoo-try-on).

pages.fontgen.seo_gothic_body: Rooted in medieval calligraphy, Old English and Gothic fonts deliver unmistakable weight, sharp diamond serifs, and high-contrast drama. Because the strokes are dense and ornate, these styles perform best at larger scales on the chest, upper back, or outer forearm—giving the ink plenty of open skin to age cleanly.
pages.fontgen.seo_chicano_body: Born from classic West Coast black-and-grey tattoo culture, Chicano lettering blends sweeping flourishes with sharp, expressive angles. It is a staple for family names, faith-based words, and memorial dates. Ask your artist to keep the filigree open and balanced so the loops stay distinct years later.
pages.fontgen.seo_cursive_body: Delicate, intimate, and endlessly versatile, cursive and fine line lettering mimics natural handwriting. It shines on smaller placements like the collarbone, ribcage, and inner wrist. Since thin strokes soften faster than bold outlines, stick to simple letterforms with clear breathing room between characters.
pages.fontgen.seo_typewriter_body: Clean, understated, and effortlessly modern, typewriter fonts bring a literary feel to single words, dates, and coordinates. Their uniform stroke weight and open spacing make them one of the most reliable choices for small-to-medium tattoos that need to stay crisp over time. pages.fontgen.d100: Can I copy and paste these tattoo fonts?
pages.fontgen.d101: Standard tattoo font copy and paste tools rely on Unicode text symbols, which look pixelated, break across devices, and cannot be used to print a clean tattoo stencil. Instead of copying plain text, our generator lets you export a crisp, high-resolution PNG or vector SVG file that your tattoo artist can resize without losing sharpness.
pages.fontgen.d102: What is the best font for a small wrist or finger tattoo?
pages.fontgen.d103: For small placements like the inner wrist, behind the ear, or fingers, choose simple, open letterforms such as Minimalist, Typewriter, or clean Block fonts. Avoid tight cursive, Chicano, or Old English script at tiny sizes—natural skin movement and ink spread will cause intricate details to blur together over time.
pages.fontgen.d104: Can I create a vertical spine or rotated lettering tattoo?
pages.fontgen.d105: Yes. Use the Rotation and Vertical toggle right below the preview window to create vertical spine tattoo lettering for spine, ribcage, or outer-forearm placements. You can also adjust the exact angle, size, and opacity before exporting your reference.
